title: Leftover Orders on a Trading Book
statement:
A tiny exchange receives orders one at a time. orders[i] = [price, amount, type] is a batch of amount identical orders at price. type is 0 for buy and 1 for sell. Orders that are not filled wait in the backlog.

  • A new buy batch trades with the cheapest waiting sell order, as long as that sell price is at most the buy price. Each trade fills one unit on both sides. It keeps trading until it is fully filled or no waiting sell is cheap enough; what is left joins the backlog.
  • A new sell batch does the mirror image: it trades with the highest waiting buy order whose price is at least the sell price.

After all batches are processed, return the total number of orders left in the backlog, modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: The sell at 12 finds no buyer. The sell at 9 fills 4 of the 5 buys at 10. The buy at 11 cannot reach the sell at 12. Left: 1 + 3 + 6 = 10.
The buy at 7 sweeps both sell levels (2 at 5, then 3 at 6) and leaves 5 of its own orders waiting.

hints: A buy always wants the cheapest waiting sell; a sell always wants the most expensive waiting buy. Which structure hands you the extreme instantly?
Keep two heaps: a min-heap of sells and a max-heap of buys, each entry a [price, amount] pair.
Trade in whole chunks: take min(remaining, top amount), reduce both, and pop the top when it reaches zero. Never loop one unit at a time.

explain.intuition:
This is a real order book in miniature. A buyer only cares about the best (cheapest) seller; a seller only cares about the best (highest) buyer. So each side of the backlog should be a priority queue keyed by price: a min-heap for sells and a max-heap for buys.

Amounts go up to 10⁹, so trade in chunks. When a buy batch arrives, look at the cheapest sell. If it is cheap enough, fill min(left, top.amount) at once, shrink both, pop the top if it is used up, and repeat. Each batch is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the whole run is O(n log n). The final sum is at most 10¹⁴, well inside the range where JavaScript numbers are exact, so summing first and taking the modulo at the end is safe.
steps: Create a min-heap sells and a max-heap buys of [price, amount].
For a buy [p, a]: while a > 0 and the cheapest sell has price ≤ p, trade min(a, top.amount), and pop the top if it reaches 0. If a > 0, push [p, a] into buys.
For a sell: the mirror image against the highest buy with price ≥ p.
Sum the amounts left in both heaps and return the sum modulo 1 000 000 007.
pitfalls: Matching with the oldest waiting order instead of the best price.
Looping one unit at a time. Amounts reach 10⁹.
Treating equal prices as no match. A buy at 5 does trade with a sell at 5.

solutions.title: Scan the backlog for the best price
solutions.idea: Keep the backlog as two plain lists. For each new batch, repeatedly scan the other list for the best price and trade in chunks.

solutions.title: Two heaps
solutions.idea: Sells in a min-heap by price, buys in a max-heap by price. Each new batch trades against the top of the opposite heap in chunks.

followups: Orders can now be cancelled by id. What extra structure do you need, and how do you handle a cancelled order still sitting in a heap?
Report the price of every trade as it happens. Which side's price should a trade use?
